newsitem.title: BELGIUM: WEDNESDAY ANOTHER CRUNCH DAY FOR BELGIAN OLOS.
newsitem.headline: WEDNESDAY ANOTHER CRUNCH DAY FOR BELGIAN OLOS.

text.p: Belgian OLOs, slightly firmer on Monday in line with Bunds which were helped by the Mark DEM= recovery against the dollar USD/N, treaded lightly ahead of the release on Wednesday of key U.S. retail sales data US-ECI.
"There is little movement, the market is waiting for the data," said analyst Koen Dierckx at Kredietbank.
Earlier data had indicated that the third quarter in the U.S. had started strongly, he said.
"The market fears that Wednesday's data will confirm this picture," Dierckx said. "They could fan fears of a strong growth and fear of inflation."
July retail sales, due at 1230 GMT on Wednesday, are seen up 0.7 percent on the month, after rising 0.5 percent in June.

The dollar's easing also dampened fears that the Bundesbank would hike rates or shift to a revisable repo rate as early as Tuesday. "The fall of the dollar removed the direct cause (for a German rate hike)," Dierckx said.
But he added that the upward trend of the dollar was left intact despite the slip to 1.86 on Monday from its recent high of 1.90.
"The underlying motives remain unchanged -- fear of a stronger U.S. economy and the threat of a weak EMU," he said.
Dealers earlier said they were convinced the Buba had set a target for a rate rise.
"But it is unclear whether it's 1.90 (marks to the dollar) or 1.95," one said.
He added however the rate rise would be the ultimate weapon and would always be preceded by intervention.
Some market rumours suggested central banks had been intervening last week by selling dollars but traders noted the rumours had remained unconfirmed.
Dierckx said the short end of the market had normalised on Monday after upward pressure had ebbed.
The Belgian franc, which had steadily been weakening to well below its ERM midrate against the mark, recovered to 20.6485/00 from 20.6505/20 DEMBEF= on Monday.

London currency analysts said last week that if the franc's weakness continued, Belgium might surprise the markets with an interest rate rise. But others wondered if Belgium -- particularly its exporters -- was not actually content to see a softer franc.
